text:
IN THE SUPREME
COURT OF BRITISH COLUMBIA

Citation:

Budgell v. British Columbia,

2007 BCSC 991

Date: 20070706

Docket:
S070019

Registry: Vancouver

Between:

Christopher J. Budgell

Plaintiff

And

Wally Oppal and Michael De Jong and
Attorney General of B.C. and B.C. Minister of Labour and John Doe and Her
Majesty the Queen in Right of the Province of British Columbia

Defendants

Before:
The Honourable Madam Justice Ross

Reasons for Judgment

Counsel for the Plaintiff

In
Person

Counsel for the Defendants

Bryant
A. Mackey

Date and Place of Hearing:

June
1, 2007

Vancouver,
B.C.

INTRODUCTION

[
1
]

This is an application brought pursuant to Rule
19(24), by the defendants, Wally Oppal, Michael de Jong, the Attorney General
of British Columbia, the British Columbia Minster of Labour and Her Majesty the
Queen in Right of the Province of British Columbia, for an order striking the
statement of claim and dismissing the action as against them on the grounds
that it:

(a)       discloses no cause of action;

(b)       is unnecessary, scandalous, frivolous, or vexatious; and

(c)        is an abuse of
the process of the court.

[
2
]

Mr. Budgell wished the record to reflect for
purposes of a possible appeal, his position that all judges of this Court are
in a position of conflict with respect to the adjudication of this claim.

FACTS

[
3
]

The plaintiff, Christopher J. Budgell, has been
a party in a series of proceedings arising from his efforts to grieve what he
asserted was a wrongful dismissal by his employer, the City of Vancouver.  The
chronology of those proceedings was summarized by Rogers J. in
Budgell v.
British Columbia (Labour Relations Board)
(2005), 138 A.C.W.S. (3d)
1085,
2005 BCSC 487
at paras.
2 to 11
as follows:

Mr. Budgell was employed by the City of Vancouver
(City) in 1998 and 1999. The City fired him from his job. Mr. Budgell thought
the firing was unjustified and grieved it though [
sic
] Local 15 of the
Canadian Union of Public Employees (Union). The grievance went to arbitration.
The arbitrator ruled against Mr. Budgell. Mr. Budgell asked the LRB to review
the arbitrator's decision. The LRB complied, and it confirmed the arbitrator.

After losing the arbitration and review, Mr.
Budgell launched a complaint against his Union. He alleged that the Union had
failed to fairly represent him in the grievance. He said this was contrary to
the Union's duty to him under s. 12 of the
Labor Relations Code
.
A s. 12 complaint must be presented to the B.C. Labor Relations Board. A
one-member panel convened by the LRB evaluated Mr. Budgell's complaint. The one-member
panel performed its gatekeeper role pursuant to
s. 13(1)
(a) of the
Code
.
The one-member panel determined that Mr. Budgell had not made out a case
because the Union had, in fact, brought his case to arbitration. The panel,
therefore, dismissed Mr. Budgell's complaint as it was mandated to do by s.
13(1)(a). That dismissal was recorded by the LRB as Decision No. B448/2000.

Mr. Budgell was unsatisfied with Decision No.
B448/2000. He requested and got an LRB panel to reconsider Decision No.
B448/2000. This reconsideration panel found that Decision No. B448/2000 erred
by dismissing the claim on the grounds it did. However, upon consideration of
the complaint anew and after hearing extensive argument from Mr. Budgell the
reconsideration panel decided that Mr. Budgell's complaint had no merit and
dismissed it pursuant to s. 13(1)(a). The reconsideration panel's decision is
recorded by the LRB as Decision No. B108/2001.

Mr. Budgell was unsatisfied with the
reconsideration Board's decision in Decision No. B108/2001. He filed a petition
for review pursuant to the
Judicial Review Procedure Act
. At the
hearing of the
Judicial Review Procedure Act
petition, Mr.
Budgell voiced numerous arguments to Mr. Justice Goepel. Goepel J. ruled for
Mr. Budgell in respect of one of those arguments, namely that it was patently
unreasonable for the Board to not find that the Union's late appointment of
outside counsel for Mr. Budgell at the arbitration hearing was
prima facie

a failure of its duty to fairly represent its member. Mr. Budgell advanced a
panoply of additional arguments before Goepel J. Those additional arguments
were unsuccessful. In the end, Goepel J., citing the one noted ground of error,
quashed the reconsideration panel's decision. Goepel J. referred Mr. Budgell's
complaint back to the LRB. Goepel J. did not order the LRB to do anything in
particular. He observed that it was for the LRB to decide what process to
employ in dealing further with Mr. Budgell's complaint against his Union.
Goepel J.'s reasons were recorded as [2003] B.C.J. No. 153,
2003 BCSC 119
. They
were handed down January 24, 2003.

The Union appealed Goepel J.'s finding that it was
patently unreasonable for the panel to not conclude that late appointment of
counsel was
prima facie
contrary to the Union's duty to fairly represent
Mr. Budgell.

While the appeal was pending Mr. Budgell agitated
for the LRB to get on with dealing with his original complaint against his
Union. He wanted progress notwithstanding that the appeal was outstanding.
Unsurprisingly, the Union plumped for delay on the theory that the appeal court
would rule for the Union, the original Board decision would be reinstated, and
that no further action on the file would be necessary or possible. Mr.
Saunders, who was by then managing the matter for the LRB, sided with Mr.
Budgell and decreed that a hearing date be fixed. That hearing date was set for
late November 2003.

On November 5, 2003, the Court of Appeal handed
down its decision. The Union prevailed - the Court of Appeal reversed Goepel J.
and reinstated the original reconsideration panel Decision of B108/2001. Mr.
Saunders then notified Mr. Budgell that the LRB did not intend to proceed with
the scheduled hearing.

Mr. Budgell was unsatisfied with Mr. Saunders'
decision. He complained. Mr. Saunders provided reasons for his decision to
down-tools and cancel the hearing. Mr. Saunders' decision was recorded as LRB
Decision No. B421/2003.

Mr. Budgell was unsatisfied with Decision No.
B421/2003. He applied to and got the LRB to reconsider Decision No. B421/2003.
The reconsideration panel confirmed the decision to not proceed with the
hearing. Although it was not required to do so, the reconsideration Board also
commented on Mr. Budgell's complaint in the first instance. The reconsideration
Board opined that if it had to rule on that complaint it would reject it and
the panel provided reasons for having come to that conclusion. The
reconsideration Board also considered Mr. Budgell's request to adduce three
items of new evidence and to argue a brand new complaint that the Union had
failed to fairly represent him. The reconsideration Board rejected Mr.
Budgell's arguments on those issues and gave reasons for doing so. The
reconsideration panel's decision was recorded as LRB Decision No. B303/2004.

Mr. Budgell was
unsatisfied with Decision No. B303/2004. He commenced this, his second petition
for review under the
Judicial Review Procedure Act
. The hearing
of that petition produced these reasons. In the course of the hearing before
this court Mr. Budgell voiced a variety of arguments, some of which were
retreads of arguments made in the proceedings culminating in the Court of
Appeal's decision, some others of which are new.

[
4
]

Mr. Justice Rogers then dismissed the
application for judicial review of the decision of the Labour Relations Board (the
“Board”) reconsideration panel.  Mr. Budgell then commenced this action.
The claim set out in the writ of summons is:

The plaintiff’s
claim against the defendants is for misfeasance in public office while performing
duties of Ministers of the Crown with respect to the unlawful exercise of
statutory powers and subsequent denial of same for the specific purpose of
injuring the plaintiff. The defendants intentionally breached their duties as
Ministers of the Crown for an improper purpose or unlawfully or with a mind of
reckless indifference to the illegality of their acts and to the probability of
injury to the plaintiff thereby causing loss of past and future wages or loss
of legal opportunities to recover the same, unnecessary legal costs, and other
financial losses, mental distress, anger, depression, anxiety and loss of
enjoyment of life. In addition, the Plaintiff says that Her Majesty the Queen
in right of the Province of British Columbia is vicariously liable for the
actions of the other defendants.

[
5
]

The statement of claim alleges:

1.         In 2005 and 2006 the Attorney
General and the Minister of Labour received from the plaintiff written
communications, including registered letters, alleging that in 1996 the government
of British Columbia surreptitiously and illegally altered Section 13 of the
B.C. Labour Relations Code to create a fraudulent and onerous “standard”, the
purpose of which was to enable the Vice Chairs of the B.C. Labour Relations
Board to dismiss without legitimate deliberation Duty of Fair Representation
(Labour Code Section 12) cases.

2.         In response to repeated
communications from the plaintiff the Attorney General and the Minister of
Labour eventually replied to the plaintiff in writing. The Minister of Labour
chose to avoid the question while the Attorney General claimed, without
providing any particulars, that there was an “appropriate” amendment of Section
13.

3.         The plaintiff alleges that:

a)         there is
no record of any amendment;

b)         staff in the Attorney General’s Legislative Counsel
Office, in concert with staff in the Ministry of Labour, used a statutory
revision process to illegally effect a substantive alteration to Labour Code
Section 13, based on language provided by the Labour Relations Board;

c)         the responses of the Attorney General and the Minister of
Labour to the plaintiff were intended to cover up the truth and to perpetuate
the resulting denial of justice.

4.         The plaintiff also alleges that the
adjudicators at the B.C. Labour Relations Board had knowingly relied upon a
fraudulent standard to prevent his Duty of Fair Representation case from
receiving a fair hearing.

5.         As a result of that denial of
justice, the true nature of which was unknown to the plaintiff the plaintiff
alleges that he was compelled to seek judicial review, resulting in a series of
stressful and futile proceedings before the Board, in the B.C. Supreme Court
and in the Court of Appeal.

6.         The plaintiff further alleges that
the wrongful dismissal which precipitated all the subsequent litigation would
not have occurred had an ultimate denial of justice not been assured; that the
plaintiff thereby suffered a permanent loss of his career; and that the
employer, the union, the Labour Board and the defendants either were or should
have been cognizant that such a result was likely.

The plaintiff claims as follows:

(a)       compensatory damages for the loss of his career and
punitive damages for the perverse actions of the defendants;

(b)       acknowledgement by the court that this is a public
interest case, that the identity of the defendants and the nature of the case
raise an apprehension of bias on the part of the court, and that the plaintiff
cannot reasonably be expected to afford counsel or adequately argue the case
without the aid of counsel; and therefore

(c)        an order
by the court granting advanced costs so that the plaintiff may retain counsel
to assist in the preparation and advocacy of this case, including any necessary
amendment of this statement of claim.

RULE 19(24)

[
6
]

Rule 19(24) provides:

At any stage of a proceeding the court may order to be struck
out or amended the whole or any part of an endorsement, pleading, petition or
other document on the ground that:

(a)       it
discloses no reasonable claim or defence as the case may be,

(b)       it is unnecessary,
scandalous, frivolous or vexatious,

(c)        it
may prejudice, embarrass or delay the fair trial or hearing or the proceeding,
or

(d)       it is otherwise an abuse of
the process of the court,

and the court may grant judgment or
order the proceeding to be stayed or dismissed and may order the costs of the
application to be paid as special costs.

1.         Rule 19(24)(a): Failure to
Disclose a Reasonable Claim

[
7
]

The test for establishing that a statement of
claim discloses no reasonable claim is that set of by Wilson J. in
Hunt v.
Carey Canada Inc.
,
1990 CanLII 90 (SCC)
, [1990] 2 S.C.R. 959 at para.
33
:

Thus, the test in
Canada governing the application of provisions like Rule 19(24)(a) of the
British Columbia
Rules of Court
is the same as the one that
governs an application under R.S.C. O. 18, r. 19: assuming that the facts as
stated in the statement of claim can be proved, is it "plain and
obvious" that the plaintiff's statement of claim discloses no reasonable
cause of action? As in England, if there is a chance that the plaintiff might
succeed, then the plaintiff should not be "driven from the judgment
seat". Neither the length and complexity of the issues, the novelty of the
cause of action, nor the potential for the defendant to present a strong
defence should prevent the plaintiff from proceeding with his or her case. Only
if the action is certain to fail because it contains a radical defect ranking
with the others listed in Rule 19(24) of the British Columbia
Rules of
Court
should the relevant portions of a plaintiff's statement of claim
be struck out under Rule 19(24)(a).

[
8
]

Rule 19(1) provides:

A pleading shall
be as brief as the nature of the case will permit and must contain a statement
in summary form of the material facts on which the party relies, but not the
evidence by which the facts are to be proved.

As noted
in
Delaney & Friends Cartoon Productions Ltd. v. Radical
Entertainment Inc.
(2005), 138 A.C.W.S. (3d) 642,
2005 BCSC 371
at
para.
9
, per Joyce J. “[a] material fact is one that is essential in order to
formulate a complete cause of action.  If a material fact is omitted, a cause
of action is not effectively pleaded.”

[
9
]

The issue is not whether the plaintiff has failed
to identify the specific causes of action or tort claims advanced.  Rather, the
Court is to examine the statement of claim to see whether the material facts
set out would, if proved, complete all the consitutent elements of causes of
action known in law: see
Alford v. Canada (Attorney General)

(1997),
1997 CanLII 868 (BC SC)
, 31 B.C.L.R. (3d) 228 (S.C.) per Brenner J. at 235 and 236.

[
10
]

The essence of the claim advanced by Mr. Budgell is
directed to a change that was made to
s. 13
of the
Labour Relations Code
,
R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 244 (the “
Code
”) in 1996 substituting
“sufficient evidence that the contravention has apparently occurred” for  “
prima
facie
” as the test to be applied by the panel at first instance in
considering a complaint of a breach of a union’s duty of fair representation.
Section 13 of the
Code
provides:

(1)  If a written complaint is made to the board that a
trade union, council of trade unions or employers' organization has contravened
section 12, the following procedure must be followed:

(a)       a
panel of the board must determine whether or not it considers that the
complaint discloses a case that the contravention has apparently occurred;

(b)       if the
panel considers that the complaint discloses sufficient evidence that the
contravention has apparently occurred, it must:

(i)         serve a notice of the
complaint on the trade union, council of trade unions or employers' organization
against which the complaint is made and invite a reply to the complaint from
the trade union, council of trade unions or employers' organization, and

(ii)        dismiss the complaint or
refer it to the board for a hearing.

(2)       If the board is satisfied
that the trade union, council of trade unions or employers' organization
contravened section 12, the board may make an order or direction referred
to in section 14 (4) (a), (b) or (d).

[
11
]

The change to the provision which is the focus
of Mr. Budgell’s concerns was made pursuant to the provisions of the
Statute
Revision Act
, R.S.B.C. 1996 c. 440.  Mr. Budgell submits that this
change was a surreptitious and illegal alteration of the legislation and that
there was no proper amendment.  He submits that the ministers who are named are
named first, because they are responsible for the actions of the ministry staff
at the time of the amendments, even though they were not the ministers at the
time; and second, because the correspondence with respect to the issue of the
amendments that was exchanged between Mr. Budgell and the ministry offices in
2005 and 2006 was deceptive and had the effect of perpetuating the situation.
He submits that as a result of the change in the legislation, his employer and
union were free to collude in his wrongful dismissal, and that he suffered loss
and damage pursuing, first, the proceedings before the Board and, then the Judicial
Review proceedings on the basis of a wrongful test.

[
12
]

In my view, the pleadings fail to disclose a
reasonable claim.  The first difficulty is that, although damage is alleged to
have been suffered because of the wrongful acts of the employer, the union and
the Board, those entities have not been made parties to the action.  It is
clear that the Crown is not vicariously liable for the actions of the Board and
its functionaries; see
Speckling v. Kearney
(2007), 156 A.C.W.S.
(3d) 351,
2007 BCCA 145
.

[
13
]

The next difficulty is that lawmakers are not
liable in damages for the effects of legislation.  An action in tort for civil
damages does not lie with respect to the liability of the Crown for damages
arising out of the enactment of laws later held to be unconstitutional.  For
example, in
Welbridge Holdings Ltd. v. Winnipeg (Greater)
,
1970 CanLII 1 (SCC)
, [1971]
S.C.R. 957, Laskin J., speaking for the Court, noted:

A municipality at
what may be called the operating level is different in kind from the same
municipality at the legislative or quasi-judicial level where it is exercising
discretionary statutory authority. In exercising such authority, a municipality
(no less than a provincial Legislature or the Parliament of canada) may act
beyond its powers in the ultimate view of a court, albeit it acted on the
advice of counsel. It would be incredible to say in such circumstances that it
owed a duty of care giving rise to liability in damages for its breach.
"Invalidity is not the test of fault and it should not be the test of
liability": see Davis, 3 Administrative Law Treatise, 1958, at p. 487.

[
14
]

In
Guimond v. Quebec (Attorney General)
,

1996 CanLII 175 (SCC)
, [1996] 3 S.C.R. 347, this principle was reiterated, together with the
proposition that this principle extends to a public official who attends to the
implementation of a law that is subsequently declared to be invalid.  Justice
Gonthier, speaking for the Court, stated at paras. 13 and 14:

... The principle was reiterated by this Court in
Central
Canada Potash Co. v. Government of Saskatchewan
,
1978 CanLII 21 (SCC)
, [1979] 1 S.C.R. 42. As
Delisle J.A. observed in his dissenting reasons in the court below, at p. 253
D.L.R.:

[Translation] In terms
of the civil law, there is no doubt that the Crown is not negligent when it
enacts a law that is subsequently declared invalid, any more than the public
official who attends to its implementation. In
Central Canada Potash Co.
v. Government of Saskatchewan

(1978),
1978 CanLII 21 (SCC)
, 88 D.L.R. (3d) 609, [1979]
1 S.C.R. 42, 6 C.C. L.T. 265, Martland J., on behalf of the court, said the
following about a government official's enforcement of legislation that is
subsequently held to be
ultra vires
(at p. [90 S.C.R.]):

In my opinion it would
be unfortunate, in a federal state such as Canada, if it were to be held that a
government official, charged with the enforcement of legislation, could be held
to be guilty of intimidation because of his enforcement of the statute whenever
a statute whose provisions he is under a duty to enforce is subsequently held
to be
ultra vires
.

Professor Cooper-Stephenson, in his text
Charter
Damages Claims
(1990), at pp. 330-32, has interpreted these cases as
establishing a "claim of right" defence to civil damages claims
arising from legislation which had been declared constitutionally invalid. He
submits that these cases endorse a qualified immunity from tort claims where
governmental actors have committed a good faith and reasonable error in enforcing
legislation which is subsequently found to violate the Constitution. Dussault
and Borgeat extend this argument to its logical conclusion stating, in their
treatise,
Administrative Law
(2nd ed. 1990), vol. 5, that
Parliament itself enjoys the immunity (at p. 177):

In our parliamentary system of government,
Parliament or a legislature of a province cannot be held liable for anything it
does in exercising its legislative powers. The law is the source of duty, as
much for citizens as for the Administration, and while a wrong and damaging
failure to respect the law may for anyone raise a liability, it is hard to
imagine that either Parliament or a legislature can as the lawmaker be held
accountable for harm caused to an individual following the enactment of legislation.
[Footnotes omitted.]

[
15
]

Thus, even if the claim were amended to plead the invalidity
of the impugned provision of the
Code
, neither present claims
against the Crown, nor the individuals could be advanced.

[
16
]

The next difficulty is that the statement of
claim does not plead the material facts essential to a cause of action for
misfeasance in public office.  In
Odhavji

Estate v. Woodhouse
,
[2003] 3 S.C.R. 263,
2003 SCC 69
[“
Odhavji

Estate
”],
Justice Iacobucci, writing for the court, identified that the underlying
purpose of the tort:

…is to protect
each citizen’s expectation that a public officer will not intentionally injure
a member of the public through deliberate and unlawful conduct in the exercise
of public functions.

[
17
]

The tort is an intentional tort whose essential
elements were described in
Odhavji

Estate

as follows at
para.
32
:

To summarize, I am of
the opinion that the tort of misfeasance in a public office is an intentional
tort whose distinguishing elements are twofold: (i) deliberate unlawful conduct
in the exercise of public functions; and (ii) awareness that the conduct is
unlawful and likely to injure the plaintiff. Alongside deliberate unlawful
conduct and the requisite knowledge, a plaintiff must also prove the other
requirements common to all torts. More specifically, the plaintiff must prove
that the tortious conduct was the legal cause of his or her injuries, and that
the injuries suffered are compensable in tort law.

[
18
]

The pleadings do not contain the material facts
necessary to establish these essential elements.

[
19
]

In the case at bar, as in
A.L. v. Ontario
(Minister of Community and Social Services)
(2006),
2006 CanLII 39297 (ON CA)
, 83 O.R. (3d) 512,
274 D.L.R. (4th) 431, 218 O.A.C. 150 (C.A.) at paras.
34 -38
, the general
allegations that the defendants committed an “unlawful exercise of statutory
powers” are not buttressed by reference to the material facts necessary to
disclose a cause of action.

2.         Rule 19(24)(b):
Unnecessary, Scandalous, Frivolous, Vexatious

[
20
]

The defendants submit that the pleadings are
also liable to be struck pursuant to Rule 19(24)(b).  In
Citizens for
Foreign Aid Reform Inc. v. Canadian Jewish Congress
(1999),
1999 CanLII 5860 (BC SC)
, 36 C.P.C.
(4th) 266, 91 A.C.W.S. (3d) (B.C.S.C.), Romilly J. discussed the requirements
for the application of Rule 19(24)(b):

¶46     The
authorities provide little guidance as to what constitutes pleadings that are
“unnecessary”, “scandalous”, “frivolous” or “embarrassing”. However some
principles do emerge.

¶47     Irrelevancy
and embarrassment are both established when pleadings are so confusing that it
is difficult to understand what is being pleaded:
Gittings v. Caneco
Audio-Publishers Inc
.
(1987),
1987 CanLII 2561 (BC SC)
, 17 B.C.L.R. (2d) 38 (B.C.S.C.). An
“embarrassing” and “scandalous” pleading is one that is so irrelevant that it
will involve the parties in useless expense and will prejudice the trial of the
action by involving them in a dispute apart from the issues:
Keddie v.
Dumas Hotels Ltd.
(1985),
1985 CanLII 417 (BC CA)
, 62 B.C.L.R. 145 at 147 (B.C.C.A.). An
allegation which is scandalous will not be struck if it is relevant to the
proceedings. It will only be struck if irrelevant as well as scandalous:
College
of Dental Surgeons of B.C. v. Cleland
(1968),
1968 CanLII 1008 (BC CA)
, 66 W.W.R. 499 (B.C.C.A.).
A pleading is “unnecessary” or “vexatious” if it does not go to establishing
the plaintiff’s cause of action or does not advance any claim known in law:
Strauts
v. Harrigan
,
1992 CanLII 595 (BC SC)
, [1992] B.C.J. No. 86 (Q.L.) (B.C.S.C.). A pleading that is
superfluous will not be struck out if it is not necessarily unnecessary or
otherwise objectionable:
Lutz v. Canadian Puget Sound Lumber and Timber
Co.

(1920), 28 B.C.R 39 (C.A.)
. A pleading is “frivolous” if it is
obviously unsustainable, not in the sense that it lacks an evidentiary basis,
but because of the doctrine of estoppel:
Chrisgian v. B.C. Rail Ltd. et
al.
,
[1992] B.C.J. No. 1567
, (6 July 1992), Prince George Registry
20714 (B.C.S.C.).

[
21
]

The defendants submit that the whole of the
pleading is unnecessary and vexatious because no part goes to establishing a
cause of action or advancing a claim known to law.  The defendants also submit
that the pleadings are so confusing that it is difficult to understand what is
being pleaded, who is alleged to be at fault and why, and which actions are the
true subject matter of the claim.

[
22
]

I have concluded that the pleadings are
irrelevant and embarrassing, as those terms have been defined by the case law.
In addition, the pleadings do not establish a cause of action or advance a
claim known to law and the claims, therefore, are unnecessary and vexatious.

3.         Rule 19(24)(d): Abuse of
Process/Collateral Attack

[
23
]

When determining whether proceedings constitute
an abuse of process, the Court may consider whether the court process is being
used dishonestly or unfairly, or for some ulterior or improper purpose.  It may
also consider whether there have been multiple or successive related
proceedings that are likely to cause vexation or oppression: see
Young v.
Borzoni
,
2007 BCCA 16
at para.
65
(citing
Lawrence v. Sandilands
,
2003 BCSSC 211 at para. 95).

[
24
]

The defendants submit that because the pleadings
make reference to the adjudicators of the Board and to the administrative law
process, the action constitutes a collateral attack on the administrative
process established under provincial legislation and is therefore an abuse of
process:
Gemex Developments Corp. v. Coquitlam (City)
,
2002 BCSC
412
at para.
21
; aff’d,
2002 BCCA 573
;
Varzeliotis (c.o.b. Alcyone News)
v. British Columbia
,
2007 BCSC 620
at paras.
46-53
;
Forest Glen
Wood Products Ltd. v. British Columbia (Minister of Forests)
,
2007 BCSC
273
;
Berscheid v. Ensign
,
1999 CanLII 6494 (BC SC)
, [1999] B.C.J. No. 1172 (S.C.).

[
25
]

Mr. Budgell submits that the action is not a
collateral attack on the administrative process, but that the essence of the
claim is in relation to the illegitimate usurpation of the exclusive mandate of
the legislature, the result of which was to render futile the proceedings
before the Board and the process of judicial review before the courts.

[
26
]

It appears to me that, to a certain extent, Mr.
Budgell is seeking similar relief in this action to the relief he sought in the
proceedings before the Board and in the Judicial Review proceedings.  For
example, in
Budgell v. British Columbia (Labour Relations Board)
,

2003 BCSC 119
rev’d,
2003 BCCA 605
, Mr. Budgell sought,
inter alia
, an
order that all wages and benefits plus interest lost by the petitioner since
his dismissal and until a decision was rendered by the new arbitration panel,
be paid by the union.  In these proceedings, he seeks an order for compensatory
damages for the loss of his career.

[
27
]

In addition, the issue of the proper test to be
applied by the Board is a matter that could have been raised before the Board
and in the course of the Judicial Review proceedings.  As Mr. Justice Drossos
noted in
Berscheid v. Ensign
,
supra
, at paras.
51 and 52
:

As a result of this distinction between judicial
review and civil litigation, a party cannot seek a remedy statutorily provided
for by judicial review through civil proceedings. Such an evasion of the
judicial review process is known as a collateral attack and is prohibited.
Where the legislature clearly intends to confer jurisdiction on an appeal
tribunal to hear and determine certain matters, the court lacks the
jurisdiction to do so:
R. v. Consolidated Maybrun Mines Ltd.
,
1998 CanLII 820 (SCC)
, [1998]
1 S.C.R. 706. It is only after the complainant has completed the statutorily
imposed administrative process that the avenue of judicial review becomes
available and, it should be noted, such judicial review is only available in
limited circumstances.

Further, where the
plaintiff has already commenced proceedings by way of petition for judicial
review under the
Judicial Review Procedure Act
to challenge the
orders of an administrative tribunal, it is an abuse of process to commence
subsequent civil proceedings seeking substantially the same remedies against
the same parties as set out in the petition.

[
28
]

In my view, Mr. Budgell sincerely believes that
earlier decisions were wrong and that he has not been treated fairly.  I do not
believe that he is pursuing this litigation dishonestly or for some improper
purpose.  It is my view, however, that the plaintiff is in the present action
seeking remedies sought in the administrative proceedings and raising issues
that were or could have been raised in those proceedings.  In
Budgell v.
British Columbia (Labour Relations Board)
,
2005 BCSC 487
, at paras.
54
to 58
Rogers J. noted:

In the course of his submissions to the Decision
No. B303/2004 panel Mr. Budgell gave the panel to understand that he would
continue to litigate his complaint so long as a legal avenue was open to him.
The panel then gave extensive reasons touching on all the arguments Mr. Budgell
raised, including arguments that went beyond the jurisdiction, new evidence,
and new complaint issues. Those additional arguments included assertions that
the LRB itself is poisoned by systemic bias against individuals who complain
about their unions and that Mr. Saunders, who wrote Decision No. B421/2003,
abused the LRB process in the time he had conduct of the matter.

While the Decision No. B303/2004 panel thought
there was utility in addressing these arguments, I do not. Neither do I think
there is utility in considering whether the panel's conclusions on those
arguments is or is not patently unreasonable. That is because any verbiage
expended by the B303/2004 panel in addition to its discussion and conclusions
on jurisdiction, new evidence, and the new complaint was pure obiter dicta.

Most particularly, given the fact that Mr.
Saunders ultimately had no jurisdiction to do anything for Mr. Budgell, the quality
of his conduct while dealing with Mr. Budgell is irrelevant. Equally irrelevant
is Mr. Budgell's argument that Mr. Saunders' was biased against him. I wholly
agree with the Decision No. B303/2004 panel's conclusion that Mr. Saunders did
not act arbitrarily or abuse the process. But since Mr. Saunders could not have
effected a change in the outcome for Mr. Budgell there is simply no point in
analyzing his conduct of the case while it was in his hands.

Further, Mr. Budgell's complaints to the B303/2004
panel and to me about systemic or institutional bias at the LRB simply
reiterate arguments he had unsuccessfully made earlier in the train of process
leading to today. His arguments were bad then and have not improved since. For
the record and to the extent that it is necessary for me to pronounce on the
topic, I can find no error in the analysis and conclusions of Goepel J. and the
Decision No. B303/2004 panel where they reject Mr. Budgell's allegations of
bias and lack or independence.

No useful purpose would
be served in picking through and disposing of Mr. Budgell's various other
arguments concerning the meaning of prima facie, the use of Hansard to
interpret the
Code
, what constitutes a hearing, whether one
academic or another has written at one time or another that the rule-of-law
ought to apply to administrative tribunals, that the LRB is somehow frightened
of fair representation complaints and organizes its affairs to avoid them, and
so on. These arguments are not germane to whether the LRB had jurisdiction to
entertain Mr. Budgell's complaint after the Court of Appeal had its say on his
case. That decision was the end of all things except for the new evidence
motions, the fresh fair representation complaint and the allegation of bias.
The Decision No. B303/2004 panel decisions on those latter issues were, for the
reasons set out above, correct.

This is another in a series of multiple,
successive related proceedings.  I agree with the submission of the defendants
that this constitutes an abuse of the process of the courts.

CONCLUSION

[
29
]

In the result, I have concluded that the
statement of claim does not disclose a reasonable claim, that the pleadings are
also unnecessary and vexatious, and that they constitute an abuse of the
process of the court.  In the result, the pleadings shall be struck and the
claim against these defendants dismissed, with costs to these defendants.

“Ross
J.”
